1. **The idea:** The frames show a grid of tiles. Each tile appears to be one starting month. Light tiles mean a buyer who held the home came out ahead. Dark tiles mean a renter came out ahead. The labels say the data comes from FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. The animation is marked "ILLUSTRATIVE", "US only" and "history, not a forecast". It compares buying with renting across past periods.

2. **What changes:** The date label stays at "January 1991" in every frame. The pattern of dark tiles changes instead. In frames 1 and 2, dark tiles form a vertical band in the middle, with a few light tiles inside it. In frames 3 and 4, dark tiles also appear along the left edge and in the lower part of the middle band. The grid is mostly light by frame 4. In frames 5 and 6 a caption appears: "held five years: buyer ahead in 74.4%". The dark pattern stays roughly the same in those last two frames.

3. **What it means:** In this historical data, buying beat renting for most starting months. The caption gives the figure as 74.4% when the home is held five years. The legend says the light tiles are for buyers ahead after ten years. The caption names a five-year hold, so I can't tell whether the grid is showing the five-year or the ten-year result. A minority of starting periods favored renting. Those are the dark clusters, which may correspond to particular market periods.

4. **Advice a viewer would take:** A viewer would probably conclude that buying has usually paid off if you stay about five years or longer. They would also see that it doesn't always pay off, because some starting periods favored renting. The "not a forecast" label tells viewers not to treat the 74.4% as a prediction.

5. **Source of that advice:** The animation shows the 74.4% figure and the "history, not a forecast" disclaimer. It does not state any advice or recommendation. The takeaway in 4 is my own conclusion from the figures. The animation also doesn't show whether interest, property tax, insurance and repairs are included, so I can't confirm it answers your cost question.
